polities.name: Late Harappan (Cemetery H phase, north-western India)
polities.capital: Type site: Harappa (Cemetery H); Indian sites: Bara, Ropar, Manda
polities.summary: As the great Indus cities faded after 1900 BC, their descendants lived on in villages across Punjab and Haryana, burying their dead in painted urns of the distinctive Cemetery H style. Visitors today can see their legacy at Ropar in Punjab and in the hundreds of Late Harappan mounds dotting the Ghaggar (Sarasvati) plain, with Manda in Jammu marking the civilisation's northernmost outpost.

polities.name: Late Harappan of Gujarat (Rangpur / Sorath Harappan)
polities.capital: Type site: Rangpur (Surendranagar); major sites: Lothal, Rojdi
polities.summary: In Gujarat the Harappan world wound down gently: the dockyard town of Lothal and villages like Rangpur and Rojdi carried on farming millets and making sturdy red pottery long after the big cities declined. Their sites remain among Gujarat's premier archaeological attractions today.

polities.name: Ochre Coloured Pottery – Copper Hoard culture
polities.capital: Type site: Sinauli (Baghpat, UP)
polities.summary: Farmers of the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab left behind fragile ochre-washed pottery and spectacular hoards of copper harpoons, swords and strange anthropomorphic figures. The royal-looking burials with wooden 'chariots' excavated at Sinauli near Delhi belong to this world and have made headlines across India.

polities.name: Ahar-Banas culture
polities.capital: Type site: Ahar (Udaipur); major site: Balathal
polities.summary: Along the Banas river of southern Rajasthan, copper-smelting villagers built stone-and-mud houses and produced striking black-and-red ware pottery, trading with the Harappans to their west. The excavated mound of Ahar sits inside modern Udaipur, and Balathal near it shows some of India's earliest fortified village life.

polities.name: Kayatha culture
polities.capital: Type site: Kayatha (Ujjain district)
polities.summary: On the Malwa plateau, the Kayatha people (c. 2100-1800 BC) lived in wattle-and-daub huts, kept cattle, and made violet-painted chocolate-brown pottery alongside copper axes and bead necklaces. Their type site lies near Ujjain, later famed in legend as the birthplace of astronomer Varahamihira.

polities.name: Southern Neolithic (ash-mound tradition)
polities.capital: Type site: Sanganakallu (Ballari); ash-mounds at Budihal, Utnur
polities.summary: Cattle-herding communities of the Deccan periodically burned vast heaps of cow dung, creating the mysterious 'ash-mounds' that still rise from the Karnataka and Andhra landscape. They ground millets, polished stone axes, and settled granite hilltops like Sanganakallu near Hampi, one of South Asia's largest Neolithic hill settlements.

polities.name: Eastern Neolithic (Chirand)
polities.capital: Type site: Chirand (Saran district, Bihar)
polities.summary: At Chirand on the Ganga near Chhapra, some of eastern India's earliest farmers grew rice, wheat and lentils and crafted delicate bone and antler tools from round mud huts. The riverside mound preserves an unbroken story of village life stretching back over four thousand years.

polities.name: Late Harappan (Cemetery H phase)
polities.capital: Type site: Harappa (Cemetery H); Indian sites: Bara, Sanghol
polities.summary: The Cemetery H folk of Punjab and Haryana cremated or urn-buried their dead beneath pottery painted with peacocks and stars, hinting at new beliefs about the afterlife. Their village mounds along the drying Ghaggar-Hakra (Sarasvati) river can still be visited across Haryana, including near Rakhigarhi.

polities.name: Late Harappan of Gujarat (Rangpur phase)
polities.capital: Type site: Rangpur; major site: Rojdi
polities.summary: Saurashtra's villages thrived on drought-hardy millets as the Harappan urban world receded, developing the glossy Lustrous Red Ware that defines Gujarat's later prehistory. Rangpur and Rojdi show how ordinary farmers kept Harappan craft skills alive for centuries.

polities.name: Ochre Coloured Pottery – Copper Hoard culture
polities.capital: Type site: Sinauli (Baghpat); hoard sites: Bisauli, Rajpur Parsu
polities.summary: Over 950 OCP sites blanket the western Ganga plain, where villagers stashed hoards of copper weapons — including the enigmatic 'anthropomorph' figures now displayed in museums in Delhi and Lucknow. A famous hoard from Bahadarabad near Haridwar ties Uttarakhand's Ganga gateway into this copper-rich world.

polities.name: Ahar-Banas culture
polities.capital: Type site: Ahar (Udaipur)
polities.summary: The Ahar-Banas villages of Mewar were at their height, smelting copper from the Aravalli hills and turning out elegant black-and-red bowls. Gilund, another of their towns, even boasted a large parallel-walled public building — a rarity for village India of this age.

polities.name: Malwa culture (early phase)
polities.capital: Type site: Navdatoli (Maheshwar, Narmada valley)
polities.summary: Succeeding the Kayatha folk, the Malwa culture spread farming villages across the Narmada valley and Malwa plateau, painting buff pottery with lively animals, dancers and sun symbols. Navdatoli, opposite the temple town of Maheshwar, is one of the largest Chalcolithic villages ever excavated in India.

polities.name: Southern Neolithic (ash-mound tradition)
polities.capital: Type site: Sanganakallu; other sites: Brahmagiri, Utnur, Nagarjunakonda region
polities.summary: Deccan herder-farmers expanded southward, carrying their millet-and-cattle way of life into the hills of Tamil Nadu (as at Paiyampalli). Their hilltop villages, ash-mounds and polished stone axes mark South India's first farming societies.

polities.name: Eastern Neolithic (Chirand)
polities.capital: Type site: Chirand (Saran district, Bihar)
polities.summary: Chirand's rice farmers flourished on the fertile Ganga floodplain, their bone tools and terracotta beads showing a self-sufficient village world far from the collapsing Indus cities. The site remains Bihar's window into its deepest agricultural past.

polities.name: Early Vedic tribes over Late Harappan substrate
polities.dynasty: Early Rigvedic janas (Purus, Bharatas and others) / final Cemetery H
polities.capital: No capital: mobile cattle-keeping clans of the Sapta Sindhu (Punjab-Sarasvati region)
polities.summary: Around this time Sanskrit-speaking pastoral clans — the janas of the Rigveda, such as the Purus and Bharatas — became established in the land of the seven rivers, mingling with the last Cemetery H villagers. They left almost no monuments, but their hymns, composed on these very plains, are the oldest living literature on Earth.

polities.name: Lustrous Red Ware culture (Late Harappan Gujarat)
polities.dynasty: Rangpur III / Lustrous Red Ware tradition
polities.capital: Type site: Rangpur (period III)
polities.summary: Gujarat's post-Harappan farmers perfected a beautiful glossy red pottery — Lustrous Red Ware — found from Saurashtra to the Gulf of Khambhat. Their modest villages are the final chapter of the Harappan story in western India.

polities.name: Late OCP – Copper Hoard culture
polities.capital: Hoard sites: Saipai (Etawah), Rajpur Parsu
polities.summary: The last OCP communities of the doab still deposited copper hoards before their tradition faded around 1500 BC, giving way to new pottery styles. Many of their gleaming harpoons and swords can be seen in the National Museum, New Delhi.

polities.name: Ahar-Banas culture (late phase)
polities.capital: Type site: Ahar (Udaipur); major site: Balathal
polities.summary: The long-lived Ahar-Banas villages entered their final centuries, still working Aravalli copper as their settlements slowly contracted. Udaipur's Ahar mound and its adjoining royal cenotaph complex make an easy half-day heritage stop today.

polities.name: Malwa culture
polities.capital: Type site: Navdatoli; Deccan sites: Daimabad, Inamgaon (Malwa phase)
polities.summary: Malwa farmers pushed south across the Tapi into Maharashtra, founding large villages like Daimabad and Inamgaon with granaries, shrines and painted pottery. Daimabad later yielded the famous bronze chariot-and-animals hoard displayed in Mumbai's CSMVS museum.

polities.name: Southern Neolithic
polities.capital: Type site: Sanganakallu; other sites: Brahmagiri, Hallur, Paiyampalli
polities.summary: The Deccan's Neolithic villages matured into sizeable hilltop communities growing native millets and pulses, with the great ash-mound burnings winding down. Sites like Brahmagiri and Hallur would soon witness South India's leap into the Iron Age.

polities.name: Eastern Neolithic–Chalcolithic transition
polities.capital: Type sites: Chirand (Bihar), Pandu Rajar Dhibi (West Bengal)
polities.summary: Eastern India's rice villages began adopting copper tools and black-and-red pottery, with Pandu Rajar Dhibi on the Ajay river marking Bengal's earliest known farming settlement. Together these sites trace the dawn of metal-using village life in the eastern Ganga plains.

polities.name: Rigvedic tribes (Bharatas, Purus and rival janas)

rulers.name: Divodasa of the Bharatas (traditional/inferred from Rigveda)

polities.capital: No capital: clan territories along the Sarasvati, Sutlej and Yamuna
polities.summary: Cattle-wealthy Vedic clans now dominated the northwest, their chiefs — like the Bharata king Divodasa remembered in the Rigveda — raiding and sacrificing across the Punjab-Haryana plains. Their world of fire altars, chariots and soma rituals shaped Hindu tradition for all time, though they built in perishable wood and left the land itself as their monument.

polities.name: Lustrous Red Ware culture
polities.dynasty: Rangpur III / Lustrous Red Ware tradition
polities.capital: Type site: Rangpur (period III); site: Prabhas Patan (Somnath)
polities.summary: Gujarat's Lustrous Red Ware villages carried on around Saurashtra's coasts, including at Prabhas Patan beside the later great temple of Somnath. Their glossy pottery is the signature of Gujarat's twilight Bronze Age.

polities.name: Malwa culture (final phase)
polities.capital: Type site: Navdatoli (Maheshwar)
polities.summary: The Malwa villages of the Narmada valley entered their last flourishing, their potters still painting bulls, deer and dancing figures on buff-slipped jars. Visitors to Maheshwar's riverside ghats stand within sight of Navdatoli, their greatest excavated settlement.

polities.name: Jorwe culture
polities.capital: Type site: Jorwe (Ahmadnagar); chief town: Inamgaon
polities.summary: From about 1400 BC the Jorwe culture spread across almost all of Maharashtra, with Inamgaon growing into a planned farming town complete with an irrigation channel, granaries and a chief's house. Its red-painted pottery and touching urn burials of children are highlights of Pune's Deccan College museum.

polities.name: Ganga Valley Black-and-Red Ware Chalcolithic
polities.capital: Type sites: Atranjikhera (UP), Chirand (Bihar), Pandu Rajar Dhibi (WB), Golbai Sasan (Odisha)
polities.summary: After the OCP faded, rice-growing villages using black-and-red pottery spread along the Ganga from the doab to the Bengal delta and coastal Odisha. These humble settlements laid the groundwork for the great cities and kingdoms that would rise here a few centuries later.

polities.name: Southern Neolithic (final phase)
polities.capital: Type site: Hallur (Karnataka)
polities.summary: The Deccan's Neolithic villagers were on the cusp of a revolution: at Hallur in Karnataka some of India's earliest iron objects appear around the end of this period. Their millet fields and cattle pens set the pattern of South Indian rural life that endures today.

polities.name: Northeastern Neolithic
polities.capital: Type site: Daojali Hading (Dima Hasao, Assam)
polities.summary: In the misty hills of the Northeast, Neolithic communities polished shouldered stone hoes and made cord-marked pottery with links to Southeast Asia and China. Sites like Daojali Hading in Assam reveal a distinct highland world of shifting cultivators, ancestral to the region's rich tribal cultures.

polities.name: Painted Grey Ware culture / Later Vedic tribes
polities.dynasty: Painted Grey Ware (PGW) tradition; Vedic janas coalescing toward the Kuru realm

rulers.name: Sudas of the Bharatas, victor of the Battle of the Ten Kings (traditional/inferred)

polities.capital: Type site: Hastinapura (Meerut district, UP)
polities.summary: Iron-using villagers making fine grey pottery painted with black designs spread across the Sarasvati-Ganga divide — the very landscape of the Mahabharata, whose Hastinapura is a PGW site. Vedic tradition remembers this broad era for king Sudas of the Bharatas, whose victory in the Battle of the Ten Kings on the Ravi paved the way for the Kuru realm centred on Kurukshetra.

polities.name: Lustrous Red Ware culture (final phase)
polities.dynasty: Late Harappan legacy / Lustrous Red Ware tradition
polities.capital: Type site: Rangpur (period III, terminal)
polities.summary: The last Lustrous Red Ware villages of Saurashtra mark the end of Gujarat's two-thousand-year Harappan legacy before a quieter Early Iron Age. Their mounds at Rangpur and Prabhas Patan close the region's Bronze Age story.

polities.name: Late Jorwe culture
polities.capital: Chief town: Inamgaon (Pune district)
polities.summary: As the climate turned drier, Jorwe farmers at Inamgaon shifted from wheat to hardy millets and from square houses to round huts, a vivid archaeological record of adaptation. Inamgaon's excavations near Pune are among the most complete portraits of prehistoric village life in India.

polities.name: South Indian Iron Age – megalithic beginnings
polities.dynasty: Early megalithic / Iron Age tradition of the peninsula
polities.capital: Key sites: Hallur, Brahmagiri (Karnataka); Adichanallur region (Tamil Nadu)
polities.summary: South India entered the Iron Age: communities began raising stone burial monuments — dolmens, stone circles and cists — with iron dagger and cattle offerings, a tradition dated as early as c. 1200 BC in northern Karnataka. Thousands of these megaliths still stand across the peninsula, from Hire Benakal's rock shelters to Kerala's umbrella-stones.

polities.name: Eastern Chalcolithic (Black-and-Red Ware villages)
polities.capital: Type sites: Chirand (Bihar), Pandu Rajar Dhibi (WB), Golbai Sasan (Odisha)
polities.summary: Copper-using rice farmers prospered along the middle and lower Ganga and the Odisha coast, working bone, shell and semi-precious stone beads. Within a few centuries their villages would grow into the cities of Magadha and Kalinga that shaped Indian history.

polities.name: Northeastern Neolithic
polities.capital: Type sites: Daojali Hading (Assam), Selbalgre (Meghalaya)
polities.summary: The hill peoples of the Northeast continued their long Neolithic tradition of jhum-style cultivation, polished stone tools and cord-impressed pottery. In the Garo and Khasi hills this deep past flows into the living megalith-raising customs still visible around villages like Nartiang in Meghalaya.
